articles.title: The dangers of politicians being "too online" - or not online enough
articles.summary: In an era when reputations can be made or broken with a single post, getting the balance right is tricky.
articles.body:
In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal".

It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election.

This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years".

More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester.

In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour.

They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube.

In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral.

Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach.

Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too.

So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky â being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections?

Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms.

By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras.

Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme.

Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine.

Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality".

"You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing."

There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him?

Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher".

And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country â barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos".

And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. Bea Timpson, a former press secretary to Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak who says she prefers "trad media" like broadcast and print, added: â"I have to accept that it's now non-negotiable to be online a bit, but you definitely can be too much."

TV and online websites remain the most used sources for news, but more and more of us say we also get news from social media, according to media watchdog Ofcom. While this is highest among 16-24 year olds at 78%, a majority of adults in every age group use social media to access news, apart from the over-65s. Even among over 75s, 22% find out what is happening in the world from social media. For politicians, this is no longer just about reaching young people â this is all voters.

Some platforms are more important than others. Even after Elon Musk's conversion of Twitter into X, you will still see MPs, spin doctors and journalists in the Westminster village scrolling through the platform, but digital strategists say "real voters" are found on other platforms. The main parties have far more followers on Facebook (four million combined), which is much more widely used overall, than X (where they have a combined 3.2 million).

Politicians have always looked abroad for policy and campaigning ideas, and social media is no different.

Those on the right seek to emulate the impact Donald Trump has on TruthSocial, while left-wing politicians look to the success of Zohran Mamdani becoming mayor of New York.

Some have even imported social media experts from overseas. In 2019 Boris Johnson hired New Zealand duo Ben Guerin and Sean Topham to run the digital campaign for the general election. They imported into UK politics the concept of "shitposting", releasing deliberately bad images in order to generate a reaction. This included posting a tweet featuring the slogan "Get Brexit Done" in Comic Sans, a font loathed by graphic designers.

There was a method in the madness. "People are more likely to engage with something if they feel like it's been written by a human, not by a committee of design experts," Guerin told me. "It's pretty easy to go viral for doing something weird and wacky, but that doesn't always advance the objectives of your campaign."

This seems to be borne out by some recent hits. Burnham's TikTok post rating pub snacks attracted a million views. Yet a less gimmicky video, straightforwardly listing the five things he said he had done in his first week as PM, got five million.

There is an inherent tension in political social media. Authenticity is key. Yet who really expects the prime minister to be shooting and uploading his own content?

Back in 2013 I wrote a story about how Cameron's Twitter account had favourited a tweet mocking William Hague from an account handle that made a crude joke about former Tory MP Norman Tebbit being injured in the Brighton bombing.

The prime minister's director of communications called me to complain about my "slapdash and crappy" reporting. My crime? Including a sentence which allowed for the possibility that someone other than Cameron had clicked on the like button by mistake. This would, apparently, spoil the magic for those that thought the prime minister was running his own account for his 500,000 followers.

We now know that Zack Polanski does indeed have his own log-ins. The leader of the Green Party in England and Wales faced criticism in May for sharing a post condemning police actions in the Golders Green attack, for which he apologised. Then in July he accepted an Instagram collaboration which included a man wearing a T-shirt featuring a cartoon guillotine and the song lyrics "we're only making plans for Nigel". Reform UK said it amounted to incitement of violence against Farage. "I'm accepting my responsibility in that I shouldn't have accepted that collaboration," Polanski said, but refused to apologise.

Reform UK's Gawain Towler, a long-time media adviser to Nigel Farage, says: "âMy big takeaway is: don't be a berk on social media, âwhich I think was Zack Polanski's big takeaway too."

Dov Forman, who helped Tory-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick grow his following from 20,000 to more than half a million with viral clips including confronting fare dodgers on the London Underground, says it is "risky" for a leader to run their own social media. But sometimes it can be a risk worth taking.

Badenoch has taken to directing her own videos, telling aides what she wants to post. She has attracted backing on X from American rappers Nicki Minaj and Azealia Banks. Those are the sort of authentic third-party endorsements politicians crave.

On the day he became prime minister, a video was released of Burnham being interviewed on the Career Ladder, a series run by Ukrainian TikToker Max Klymenko who interviews guests about their career, while standing on a ladder. "If they personally haven't seen the channel it's sometimes quite difficult to make sense for them," Klymenko says. Burnham had seen the show, and did use the ladder.

Which leads us to the big question: Does any of this actually work? Emma Connolly, an academic who has researched this at the Digital Speech Lab at UCL, isn't sure. "We don't necessarily have really strong evidence or convincing evidence that it could really persuade or transform the opinion of opponent voters or even those that are undecided," she says.

Young adults are taking prescription drugs instead of alcohol - and it's dividing experts

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence? Published 14 August

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise Published 6 August

Why phones on loudspeaker may become just another noise

And this in turn raises the question of how long the Burnham digital honeymoon might last. Can a prime minister TikTok his way through a war, terror attack or controversial court case? Announcing a new giveaway may go viral, but what about the details of the cuts to pay for it?

The truth is none of this is new, as Hyman explains: "The politicians who get this wrong think that social media is now the only place to be, and a substitute for doing the hard work and the heavy lifting of actually getting the right policy, getting the right narrative, and telling that story properly," he says. "Politics is about winning arguments."

After all, politicians have always wanted to be liked. It's just these days they can see it instantly if you hit that heart button on your feed.

articles.title: Iran taps financial lifeline, Russian arms as Trump escalates 'crushing' economic warfare
articles.summary: Iran is deepening ties with Russia and China through BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization to blunt U.S. sanctions, analysts warn.
articles.body: Tehran is deepening its financial and military ties with Beijing and Moscow, forging a critical lifeline as it seeks to circumvent U.S. sanctions and weather Washington’s renewed "maximum pressure" campaign, regional security analysts warned Wednesday. As the U.S. continues to ramp up Operation Economic Fury, Iran, they say, has turned to non-Western blocs and alliances to unite further with Russia and China while positioning itself as a "linchpin" in a network that directly challenges American influence. The warning came as President Donald Trump announced Wednesday what he called the "most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country," threatening sweeping consequences for nations and businesses that provide Iran with an economic lifeline as he seeks to further isolate Tehran. "This will be Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale," Trump said in a post shared on Truth Social. IRAN DEAL CLOCK HITS ZERO AS TRUMP DEMANDS ‘WHITE FLAG’ WITH NEW PRESSURE CAMPAIGN LOOMING "The Islamic Republic is looking to survive, but in order to survive, it needs to adapt," Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital. "It needs to adapt not just to U.S. and Israeli military pressure, but this U.S. political and economic pressure. "There's no doubt the Islamic Republic is looking to maximize its enmeshment with countries like Russia and China that have been subject to U.S. political and economic pressure in the past." BRICS, an economic bloc consisting of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and several recent expansion nations, and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), a Eurasian political, economic and security alliance led by Beijing and Moscow, have become key vehicles for Iran’s outreach of late. Trump has previously labeled BRICS policies "anti-American," CNBC reported. CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN Abdolnaser Hemmati, governor of the Central Bank of Iran, said Tehran will soon join the BRICS-backed New Development Bank, though the bank told Reuters it could not confirm Iran’s membership. "The most important result of cooperation among BRICS member countries is the establishment of the New Development Bank, and our country will soon become a member of this bank," Hemmati said, according to state media. "You can see Iran trying to benefit from its role in BRICS, as well as a constellation of other organizations, that really would allow itself to be shielded — or try to make itself more shielded — from U.S. political and economic pressure," Taleblu explained. "The Islamic Republic is looking to be more formally integrated into economic orders brought about by Russia and China, which are looking to contest the U.S. dollar as much as they're looking to contest U.S. power and influence. "It is quite key and important for policymakers in Washington to wake up and see how interconnected these state threats are becoming. IRAN TURNS TO PUTIN AS US TALKS COLLAPSE, HORMUZ STANDOFF THREATENS GLOBAL OIL FLOW "These are independent relationships that have been coming together. They have differences, but as an authoritarian axis, these are countries that are better able to manage their differences at present than it seems like America and the liberal western order are able to handle their differences." NBC News also reported Aug. 17 that Russia is supplying Iran with ammunition, drone components and TNT via Caspian Sea shipping routes, citing a European government document verified by a Western official. The report comes amid indications that Tehran is relying on Russian technology and military support to adapt to U.S. military and economic pressure. "Even limited technology and military flows from Russia to the Islamic Republic help it fight to survive, adapt and live another day to combat the U.S. order in the region," Taleblu said. "In the short term, there is less transaction cost on this anti-American authoritarian order that is fast emerging than there is on the pro-American order." TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA Taleblu also highlighted Iran’s dual role in what he terms the "Axis of Aggressors," a coalition of hostile, authoritarian states including Russia, China and North Korea, and the "Axis of Resistance," Tehran’s network of regional proxy groups including Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Shiite militias in Iraq. "They all have hostile intentions towards the U.S. and the liberal world order. They are authoritarians at home and creditors abroad. He also noted that even if Tehran’s economic goals within BRICS fail to fully materialize, the political and military backing it gets from Moscow and Beijing is significant. "So, even if what the Islamic Republic wants from the BRICS countries, particularly the likes of Russia and China, doesn't happen, that doesn't mean that political, economic and military support to this regime at a critical time is not happening. "The linchpin between the state threats that the U.S. faces in the 21st century, from the Axis of Aggressors and the non-state threats in the Middle East, is the Islamic Republic of Iran," Taleblu clarified. articles.title: Tens of thousands still without power in Indiana a week after deadly storms
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of people in northwest Indiana remained without power Wednesday, more than a week after deadly storms leveled trees and knocked down power lines across the region.
articles.body: Tens of thousands of people in northwest Indiana remained without power Wednesday, more than a week after deadly storms leveled trees and knocked down power lines across the region. Northern Indiana Public Service Co. said crews were working nonstop to fix the outages, but 75,000 customers still lacked electricity by late afternoon, mostly in Lake County next to the Illinois border. They included more than 20,000 customers in Gary, where residents lined up again at community centers for hot meals and a place to charge phones. The latest news for Gary wasn’t good: Full restoration is not expected there until Aug. 25, NIPSCO said. Roughly 300 poles and 44 power transmission poles need to be repaired or replaced in Gary as a result of the storm, which carried winds of 99 mph, said Melody Birmingham, an executive at NIPSCO’s parent company. Birmingham acknowledged the “real burden” of losing perishable food and people living for days without air conditioning after a “historic storm” that initially left 300,000 customers in the dark. “These aren’t simple repairs,” Birmingham said at a news conference. “These are systems that are being rebuilt.” Utility says low-income residents are not ignored Jeremy Spurrier, 51, said he’s fortunate to have a generator at his Portage home, about 40 miles southwest of Chicago. But the generator is expensive — it goes through about $75 of gas a day — and Spurrier said his family is relying on nonperishable food like soup. He drives to Illinois to get ice to chill his insulin. “If I run out of ice, that’s several hundred dollars of insulin just ruined,” he said. Gary, a majority-Black city, has been especially hit hard, with some residents voicing frustration that they’re being ignored. Birmingham denied that low-income residents were being overlooked and blamed posts on social media. “We have areas that are probably affluent where we still have customers out as well. ... This has nothing to do with race or any type of division,” said Birmingham, who is Black. “It’s really a matter of where the storm hit.” Gary Mayor Eddie Melton acknowledged that locals were “frustrated and exhausted” but said more than 600 linemen were working to restore power in the city. “I want to reiterate this is clearly not just a Gary situation. It is a northwest Indiana situation,” Melton said. No storm damage — but no power A 4-year-old boy, three men and three women were among those who had died since the storms began Aug. 11, said Liz Woods, a spokesperson for the state Department of Homeland Security. In Whiting, Myra Carden, 74, said her home wasn’t damaged by the storm — “not even a chair was blown over in the yard.” But she was in her second blackout Wednesday. Carden, her son and three dogs lost power for more than two days last week. Then the electricity went out again Tuesday. “More than once I have put in an outage report,” she said. ”All I get back is, ‘You already put in a report.’ Well, what do you want me to do? ... This doesn’t make sense. Of course I’m not a lineman; I’m a paralegal.” Carden uses a generator to keep the refrigerator humming but only when someone’s home to monitor it. “We have a deep freeze in the garage packed full with beef and chicken. I’m sure everything will be thrown away,” she said.

articles.title: Lily Hooper: Missing teen hiker found dead in Australian bush after eight-day search
articles.summary: The state premier initially said Lily Hooper had been found alive before police confirmed her death.
articles.body:
The body of a woman has been found in Australian bushland, following an eight-day search for a Sydney teenager reported missing last Wednesday.

Police said that while the body was yet to be formally identified, it was believed to be that of 18-year-old Lily Hooper. The confirmation came after the state premier told the New South Wales parliament that she had been found alive before later retracting the statement.

The teenager left her home in Sydney to go walking in a nearby national park on 12 August. Her family reported her missing later that night, after she failed to return home by 22:00.

Her car was found in a car park at the bottom of a challenging trail in the Nattai National Park.

Police said that the body was found in the Southern Highlands at approximately 11:30 local time on Thursday. Hooper's body had been found in dense vegetation and would likely have to be carried out on foot.

There was initial confusion as to Hooper's condition, after New South Wales Premier Chris Minns told a parliamentary hearing that she had been found alive. Local media suggested that her family had also been informed that she was alive.

Minns corrected himself shortly afterwards, and told the hearing that "Lily's body has been found" and she was deceased.

"This is obviously devastating, and I'm profoundly sad for her family and for all those concerned," said Minns, and apologised to the committee.

The New South Wales police commissioner Mal Lanyon told reporters that he "unreservedly" apologised for the "miscommunication".

In a press conference on Thursday afternoon, Assistant Police Commissioner Joseph Cassar did not directly respond to questions as to how Hooper's family came to be told she had been found alive.

He told reporters that there was a period of between eight to 10 minutes before the teenager's parents were given an updated report on her condition.

He said he did not know exactly what was said to the Hooper family, but that if he "could turn the clock back, I would certainly".

A multi-agency search for the missing bushwalker had taken place over the past week, with support from multiple NSW Police Force units including PolAir, the Rescue Unit, the Trail Bike Unit, the Mounted Unit and the Dog Unit.

Police have also been supported by the Rural Fire Service, the National Parks and Wildlife Service and almost 100 members of the Australian Defence Force.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese paid tribute to the 18-year-old in parliament, calling Hooper's death an unspeakable tragedy.

"Lily Hooper had so much more to offer the world. Her passing, I have no doubt, will be felt very deeply," he said.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor, Hooper's local MP, said the initial incorrect reports that Hooper had been found alive made the family's loss even worse.

"We can only imagine what Lily's family is going through right now. Such news would be a nightmare for any parent, and we grieve for Lily's wider family," Taylor said.

articles.title: Founder of collapsed Chinese property giant Evergrande sentenced to life in prison
articles.summary: Hui's sentencing marks a key moment in the fallout from Evergrande's collapse, which shook China's property sector.
articles.body:
The founder of Evergrande, the property giant at the centre of China's housing market slump, has been sentenced to life in prison and had all of his personal property confiscated.

Hui Ka Yan pleaded guilty in April to several charges, including embezzlement of assets and corporate bribery.

Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court also fined his former companies a total of 15.82bn yuan (£1.73bn; $2.35bn) over multiple crimes, including falsifying records and concealing debt.

Hui's sentencing marks a key moment in the fallout from Evergrande's collapse, which shook China's property sector and hit investors and domestic banks hard.

Hui and his businesses "seriously disrupted" the Chinese property market, resulting in significant economic losses, the court said.

Other Evergrande executives, including Hui's two sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe, were also sentenced to jail terms ranging from 22 months to 18 years, according to state media.

Once ranked Asia's richest man, Hui has seen his wealth and influence dwindle as his company unravelled.

Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin, rose from humble beginnings in rural China, where he was raised by his grandmother before venturing into property development and setting up Evergrande in 1996.

He oversaw the company's rapid rise through an aggressive expansion programme funded with large amounts of borrowed money.

Evergrande became China's biggest real estate developer, with a stock market valuation of more than $50bn (£36.7bn). Hui was once estimated to be Asia's richest person .

Evergrande: Why should I care about the crisis-hit Chinese property giant?

Anxious Chinese home buyers reel from Evergrande crisis

Crisis-hit China Evergrande ordered to liquidate

The firm was dealt a huge blow when Beijing introduced measures in 2020 to control debt in the country's property sector.

As the company struggled to meet interest payments on its debts it sold properties at huge discounts to stay afloat before collapsing in 2021.

In April, the court heard that the company had taken millions of dollars in pre-sale funding from potential house buyers that were not used for construction.

The money had instead been channelled to new property developments, resulting in hundreds of unfinished projects.

In March 2024, Hui was fined $6.5m and banned from China's capital market for life for his company overstating its revenue by $78bn .

Evergrande's stock market valuation shrank by 99% before its shares were removed from the Hong Kong exchange in August 2025 after more than a decade and a half of trading.

Evergrande's implosion has often been blamed for triggering a broader slump in China's property market that continues to weigh heavily on the economy.

At its height, Evergrande was the biggest firm in the country's real estate industry, which made up about a third of China's gross domestic product at the time.

The property market was a significant driver of growth and an important revenue source for local governments.

The industry's ongoing problems have weighed heavily on the world's second largest economy as several other major developers faced financial woes.

articles.title: Ukraine war chronicled in 50-metre-long painting
articles.summary: Gloucester's response to the war plays a huge role in the painting, artist Russell Haines says.
articles.body:
A 50-metre-long (164ft) painting depicting a city's response to the war in Ukraine is going on display for a month before being taken to the Eastern European country.

Gloucester artist Russell Haines has been painting Lines of Resistance, which chronicles the stories of Ukrainian families who found a new home in the city and residents who volunteered to deliver aid.

The painting is not finished, as Haines said "the story belongs to more than one artist". During the exhibition, which launches on Thursday, he will invite visitors to add their own words for the people of Ukraine.

Ukrainian people will have the opportunity to send messages to Gloucester residents when the painting arrives there.

Residents left without water after pipe bursts

Haines has been working on the painting in a unit at The Shirt Factory in Derby Road.

The artwork also tells the story of "aid workers, artists, soldiers and ordinary people I have met through my journeys across Ukraine", he said.

Visitors will be able to see the painting and add to it for a month from Thursday.

Children, families, community groups, Ukrainian refugees and Gloucester residents are all being invited to add to the painting.

"People can write their own messages of friendship, hope, resistance, peace and solidarity directly onto the painting," Haines said.

Haines added: "When Lines of Resistance goes to Ukraine, the messages written in Gloucester will travel with it — carrying the voices of our city across borders and reminding people thousands of miles away that they have not been forgotten."

Eventually the painting will return to Gloucester, covered in messages from Ukraine.

Speaking about his inspiration for the artwork, Haines said: "Gloucester came together and sent truckloads of aid [to Ukraine] and did some amazing things and I just wanted to celebrate what Gloucester did."

articles.title: Erin Patterson appeal: Mushroom killer must stay in jail forever for 'truly dreadful' crime, prosecutors say
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Erin Patterson's sentence was "manifestly inadequate" as it allows for the possibility of parole.
articles.body:
An Australian court has been told that the crimes of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson were "truly dreadful" and that she should never be allowed to leave prison.

Crown prosecutors are appealing against a sentence they call "manifestly inadequate" as it allows for the possibility of parole.

Patterson was jailed for life after killing three of her relatives and trying to kill another by serving them a beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms at her Victoria home in 2023.

The 51-year-old, who attended the Court of Appeal via video link from prison, will be eligible to be freed after 33 years.

The Court of Appeal in Melbourne has also heard a challenge from Patterson's lawyers as they try to overturn her convictions.

The judges say they will reserve their decisions, meaning it will likely be weeks or months before the outcome of both appeals is known.

Patterson's victims include her in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, 66, who all died after what prosecutors called "shocking illnesses" as a result of the poisoning.

The only surviving guest, Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, has never fully recovered from his ordeal, they said.

Outlining why Patterson's crime was so "dreadful", they talked of the "betrayal of trust" of family members whom she had invited for lunch.

It was, they said, the culmination of a plan she had "orchestrated " for months , including finding and preparing enough death caps to kill and "concocting a fantastic lie" to explain the lunch.

"The lunch guests had been good to the respondent and her children over many years," prosecutors said. "Not only did the respondent sit by and watch her victims consume the deadly meal over chit-chat and banter, but the meal ended with a prayer for her, following her lie about having been diagnosed with cancer. "

As the guests lay critically ill, Patterson did not admit to using foraged mushrooms, choosing instead to lie to police and health workers.

"Even when she knew that some of the victims were on life support, she maintained her lies," the prosecutors said.

At sentencing in September last year, Justice Christopher Beale said he was giving Patterson a glimmer of hope of release, solely because of her "harsh" prison conditions, telling her "there is a substantial chance that, for your protection, you will continue to be held in solitary confinement for years to come".

But the prosecutors say this was "overstated", arguing her conditions would improve over time, especially as her notoriety faded.

In court, prosecutor Brendan Kissane listed the activities open to Patterson in prison, including an exercise yard and access to hobbies including crocheting. According to reporters in court, at this point, the triple murderer closed her eyes and shook her head.

While prosecutors say Patterson should never be freed, they argue that if the appeal court disagreed, then it should at least increase the minimum sentence – calling 33 years "manifestly inadequate".

The minimum term open to the judge for the offences was 30 years. In written arguments, they said an additional three years "utterly fails to reflect the gravity of the offending or vindicate the dignity of each of the four victims".

Arguing for the punishment to be left as it was Patterson's lawyers said the judge's reasoning had been "impeccable" and had "clearly taken into account all relevant considerations" and "made appropriate findings about how serious this matter was".

Earlier on Thursday prosecutors wrapped up their challenges to Patterson's appeal to have her convictions thrown out.

Patterson's lawyers had argued last year's trial was undermined by a "catastrophic" mix-up that led to the jury staying at the same hotel as prosecutors and a key witness, and that some evidence in the trial was too speculative to have been put before the jury and caused a miscarriage of justice.

articles.title: U.S. to send hospital ship to Peru as El Niño threat looms
articles.summary: The hospital ship USNS Comfort will arrive in the northern Pacific coast of Peru in February, when El Niño is expected to peak.
articles.body: LIMA, Peru — The United States will send a military hospital ship to Peru’s Pacific coast next year to help Peru cope with the effects of the El Niño climate phenomenon as part of a broader collaboration with the South American country, U.S. Ambassador to Peru Bernie Navarro announced Wednesday. The announcement comes after Navarro met with Peruvian Foreign Minister Carlos Espá in Miami to discuss cooperation, and at a moment when the U.S. has sent increased humanitarian aid for earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela. The U.S. is also ramping up its joint military operations in the region. Espá indicated that a road map had been developed, which includes assistance in the form of equipment, expertise and overflights to prevent, mitigate and respond to the phenomenon. The amount of U.S. aid was not disclosed. Espá also met with U.S. business leaders interested in investing in mining and infrastructure projects. Navarro said in Spanish that the meeting’s objective was to understand Peru’s needs and how to provide support with a rapid response. He noted that aid following the recent earthquake in Colombia would have been faster with better coordination. Navarro indicated that the hospital ship USNS Comfort, which was already in Peru in 2018 and 2019, will arrive off the northern Pacific coast of Peru in February 2027, when El Niño is expected to peak. The El Niño climate phenomenon is a warming of the Pacific Ocean near the equator that affects global weather patterns. According to meteorologists, it could soon equal or surpass the 1997 phenomenon, which caused damage from heat waves, heavy rains, floods and forest fires. President Keiko Fujimori, who took office on July 28, has said that addressing the potentially catastrophic climate phenomenon is a priority.

articles.title: Former kindergarten teacher, 93, found dead as Hawaii residents clean up after storm
articles.summary: Hurricane Lala tore roofs off houses, uprooted trees and left many households without electricity for days.
articles.body: HONOLULU — A beloved former kindergarten teacher who taught generations of residents in a small town on Hawaii’s Big Island was one of two people whose deaths authorities blamed on a hurricane that lashed the state over the weekend with heavy rain and strong winds. May Doi, 93, was found dead Monday after she was reported missing, police said. Neighbors think she was escaping floodwaters in her home and trying to get to a nearby shelter, said ʻĀina Akamu, a former student of Doi’s who is now a vice principal at a local school. She taught for so long at Naalehu Elementary on the island’s southern tip that “Mrs. Doi was my dad’s kindergarten teacher,” Akamu said Wednesday. “She taught grandkids of her students,” he said. “She was a fixture in this community.” Akamu often saw her taking walks around the small, rural, sugar plantation-era town: “She was so strong.” He recalled how everyone looked forward to having Mrs. Doi as a teacher because she sometimes allowed students to have sleepovers in her classroom. Her deceased husband was a math teacher, Akamu said. The body of a man in his 60s was located by residents in a pasture on Tuesday, a day after police were asked to conduct a welfare check, police said. Authorities said it was the second death attributed to the storm and have not yet released his identity. Residents were struggling to clean up after Hurricane Lala tore roofs off houses, uprooted trees, covered roads in mud and rock and left many households without electricity for days. On top of all that, forecasters warned of the likelihood of another tropical cyclone forming southeast of the islands. ‘We just ask the ancestors to protect us’ Akamu also lamented the destruction of two cemeteries, including one where Akamu’s ancestors have been buried since 1850. Caskets were sticking out of the ground through the town, home to about 800 people, and headstones littered the roadway, he said. “Our graveyard is now scattered all over the community and how do we heal from that?” he said. He worries crews working to clear roads could inadvertently run over remains. “Don’t clear the road, my grandma could be in there,” he said. “That’s what makes me most emotional, it’s like you lost them again.” Akamu was trying to focus on helping his community recover by setting up a hub where residents can get donated items. They are in most need of generators, gasoline and propane, he said. “We just ask the ancestors to protect us,” Akamu said of the threat of another storm. Now well west of Hawaii’s main islands, Lala has reached major Category 3 strength with top sustained winds of 115 mph on Wednesday in what the National Hurricane Center called the first major hurricane of 2026 in the Central Pacific Ocean. But Hawaii residents were put on notice for another storm system, located far to the east-southeast. The hurricane center said conditions appeared conducive for a tropical depression to form within days. It’s too early to tell the exact location or potential wind, rain and storm surge impacts. However, “interests in the Hawaiian Islands should closely monitor the progress of this system,” the hurricane center said, adding it could be a hurricane when it moves near or over the islands by the weekend. Power repairs could take weeks Work continued to clear away tons of mud and debris left behind by a torrent of water that inundated buildings, some of whose roofs were sheared off by the winds. Dozens of homes were washed from foundations, bridges were damaged and a collapsed section of a two-lane road had cut off access to the community of Pahala. The U.S. Department of Transportation approved an initial $6 million in emergency relief to help repair transportation infrastructure damaged by Lala, U.S. Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii said. The heaviest recorded rainfall, 43.54 inches, occurred in Laupahoehoe on the northeast coast of the Big Island, the National Weather Service said. About 17,000 customers on the Big Island remained without power on Wednesday, the Hawaiian Electric utility said. Some customers on the islands of Oahu and Maui were still in the dark. Repairs in the heavily damaged areas of the Big Island, including the southern end, could take at least two weeks, the utility said. Lala was moving to the northwest at 10 mph and was expected to turn toward the north early Thursday. It was bearing down on a remote area at the northwestern edge of the Hawaiian Archipelago. Hurricane warnings were posted for portions of the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument from Lisianski Island to Maro Reef. The weather service said the storm was forecast to veer east of the Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge. The population in one of the most remote places on Earth consists entirely of a few dozen U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service staff, volunteers and contractors. Forecasters said there were no tropical-related advisories for the Midway Atoll and any impact might include some elevated surf with a limited amount of rain.

articles.title: Harvest price hike hits business with 1500% increase in bills
articles.summary: Richard Haldenby says his average monthly bill for Harvest had risen from $130 (Â£95.50) to $2,110.
articles.body:
Customers have shared their outrage after an app used by many businesses to track timesheets and produce invoices hiked bills by as much as 1500%, with one person calling it "daylight robbery".

Richard Haldenby, head of UK consultancy firm Salentis, told the BBC his monthly bill had risen from $130 (Â£95.50) to $2,110.

Others have reported similar price hikes online, with one person , external in the US saying their annual charge went from $2,800 to $23,000.

A Harvest spokesperson said customers on "outdated" legacy plans, some dating back to 2011, faced larger price increases as the product became "a significantly more powerful" tool.

They added customers are notified "30 days" by email and then "10 days before their renewal date" and can switch plans "in one click" or request help finding a better price.

Harvest was acquired by the Italian tech company Bending Spoons in 2025, and changed its pricing structure the following year.

Many businesses who pay annually are only now finding out about the increase, as their payment is now coming up for renewal.

Haldenby, whose business consists of up to 15 staff in the UK at any one time, with sister companies also in the US and Australia, said he was "in shock" when he received an email detailing the price changes.

"We have used Harvest in our three companies for at least 15 years and have been loyal and enthusiastic advocates of it," he said.

"But if we were to accept this increase it would double our IT spend for the year, which is completely unaffordable."

Until the change, businesses paid a flat monthly fee for each user.

They could add or remove users as their staffing needs changed, meaning they only paid for the people who needed access.

Under the new usage-based pricing model, businesses can also be charged according to the number of active projects, clients and tasks they have - as well as the amount of revenue they invoice through the platform.

Haldenby said he contacted the company to say his firm would not accept the change.

He was then offered a discount for the next year - taking the price down to $1,309 - which would need to be paid up front.

But he said he believed this would just "delay the inevitable", so he is "planning to migrate to a similar but less good service".

"It's a classic example of corporate greed over valuing customers," he said.

The move has drawn criticism online, with one analyst telling the BBC it was "extremely bad practice".

"Harvest has completely failed at the transparency test," said Mark Peacock, head of the UK consultancy firm PriceMaker, which focuses on pricing strategy for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

"There is no way for a customer to work out how much it's going to cost them until they get their bill at the end of the month.

"Many users are reporting a 10-fold increase in costs which is entirely unacceptable."

Damian Foks, head of consulting at Valueships, said the Harvest price hike was "a clear sign of a shift in the company's strategy from growth to monetization".

He said this was "likely" a result of the firm being taken over by new owners.

Bending Spoons has acquired more than 50 major tech firms since it was founded in 2013, such as Evernote, Vimeo and WeTransfer.

The business has a track record of raising prices in companies it has acquired in the past.

Following its 2022 acquisition of the note-taking app Evernote, the company implemented sharp subscription price increases alongside layoffs in the US and Chile.

Both WeTransfer and Vimeo have faced tighter limits on free tools since they were separately acquired by the Italian tech firm, with legacy users also forced to move onto more expensive pricing tiers.

Are you affected by the issues raised in this story? Let us know.

articles.title: John Swinney defends Â£45,000 business-class flights to World Cup
articles.summary: The Scottish government spent almost Â£100,000 on official visits to the United States in June.
articles.body:
John Swinney has defended the use of more than Â£45,000 of public funds on business-class flights for him and two senior aides to the World Cup.

Scotland's first minister flew to Boston on 11 June for Scotland's opening match, before taking part in trade talks in Kentucky three days later.

While he and two senior officials travelled business class, Sports Minister Maree Todd and several other officials went to the US on significantly cheaper economy-class flights.

Swinney insisted the government had sought to "minimise" costs, while Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the business class flights as a means of ensuring ministers "arrive fresh" when they travel overseas.

In total, the government spent Â£98,442 on trips for Swinney, Todd and their officials to the US, including flights, hotels and expenses.

Flights for Swinney and his private secretary John Webster cost Â£17,893 each.

Business-class tickets for the first minister's special adviser Colin McAllister cost Â£9,864.

The government spent a further Â£11,800 on economy-class flights for several officials accompanying Swinney, as well as more than Â£10,000 on car hire for the first minister's visit.

The cost of plane tickets for Todd and four accompanying officials to visit Miami for Scotland's final game was Â£5,485.

The Scottish government's travel rules , external state that business-class flights should only be used on flights of more than 10 hours "unless otherwise agreed".

Direct flights from Edinburgh to Boston typically last about seven hours.

Swinney told BBC Scotland News: "Obviously, when flights have got to be booked, when there's intense pressure on the time involved, then the costs are likely to be higher."

He added: "We tried to minimise those costs."

Earlier, Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the use of business-class flights.

He told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast : "These are busy trips for ministers and it is right that they are able to arrive fresh, they're able to arrive in a way that means that they're able to participate and do their work immediately, so I think that's a proportionate use."

Gray pointed to benefits of the trip, such as increasing Scotland's "soft-power reach and the ability to make significant international connections".

He added: "It was right that the first minister and his team were there to participate and to be part of that."

Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn, speaking at the BBC's Scotcast live show at the Edinburgh Festival, also defended Swinney.

He said: "If we want our politicians to go and sit in row 46 beside the toilets and then land in Boston and then go and engage with US government officials having done so we'll get exactly what we deserve as politicians."

Releasing the travel expenses, the government said the US trips were made to support the national team at the World Cup as well as to hold talks on trade, tourism, culture and investment.

Conservative MSP Stephen Kerr said: "Nobody begrudged SNP ministers joining the Tartan Army to cheer on Scotland men's team at their first World Cup appearance in nearly three decades, but in typical SNP fashion costs were never kept under control.

"Swinney and his ministerial colleague were clearly happy to escape all the challenges facing them back home, but they should have met these significant costs out of their own pocket."

articles.title: China puts AI 'robocops' on traffic duty; one 'Superman' robot claims to be faster than Usain Bolt
articles.summary: China News: China is putting robots to work in real-world policing, with a traffic-control machine in Hangzhou now issuing warnings to motorists and pedestrians. .
articles.body: China is putting robots to work in real-world policing, with a traffic-control machine in Hangzhou now issuing warnings to motorists and pedestrians. Meanwhile, another Chinese robotics firm has unveiled a humanoid machine whose claimed top speed exceeds Usain Boltâs 100-metre world-record pace.At a busy intersection in Hangzhou, the 1.88-metre, 98-kg T2 robot, developed by SUPCON Information, is being deployed to handle routine traffic-control duties. The machine uses cameras, radar and onboard computing to identify helmetless e-bike riders, passengers on e-bikes, vehicles crossing stop lines and pedestrians violating signals.The robot has no power to arrest and does not carry a gun. Instead, it can issue warnings, answer questions about directions, parking and traffic rules, and connect users with police in emergencies.âThe robots can also answer questions about directions, parking and traffic rules,â Cao Hui, head of SUPCONâs intelligent unmanned systems innovation centre, told Reuters. Its seven-jointed arms can reproduce standard traffic-police gestures in sync with traffic signals.SUPCON has deployed 15 robots in Hangzhou since May and says they have issued more than 170,000 warnings. The company also claims monthly cases of helmetless riding and vehicles crossing stop lines have fallen by more than 40 per cent. However, the figures could not be independently verified.Cao said the robots can operate for long periods without fatigue. âIt doesn't get tired,â he told Reuters, adding, âIt can work steadily for long periods.âThe machines operate autonomously from 7 am to 6 pm, moving between preset positions, while a central platform allows traffic-police teams to monitor and dispatch them.SUPCON says nearly 50 such robots are now operating across about eight cities in three Chinese provinces, with deployments expected to approach 200 by the end of the year.Chinaâs wider robotics push has also produced a viral moment involving Unitreeâs new humanoid robot, âSupermanâ.Unitree said on X that the robot was âSurpassing the standing high jump and running speed records of all humans around the worldâ. At that speed, its claimed pace would exceed Boltâs world-record 100-metre average speed if sustained throughout the distance. However, the machine has not actually raced Bolt or broken his official record.Unitree said âSupermanâ had been developed for just over three months, with scope for further improvements. The company claims the robot can achieve a 2-metre standing high jump and a top speed of 12.66 metres per second, with a leg length of 0.85 metres.However, the performance claims have not been independently verified. Meanwhile, several viral videos circulating online also show the robot crashing into a wall after appearing to lose its direction.As China pushes robots from demonstrations into traffic management and other practical roles, overseas deployment could prove more complicated. articles.title: Retro Pizza Hut draws customers from hours away as 1980s nostalgia sends sales soaring
articles.summary: Retro appeal has turned a small-town Pizza Hut into a destination for customers seeking a nostalgic dining experience, with its franchise operator planning to add even more throwback touches.
articles.body: Florida's only Pizza Hut Classic, featuring the nostalgic red plastic cups, vinyl booths, Tiffany-style lamps and checkerboard tablecloths reminiscent of the 1980s, has become so popular that employees from other locations have been brought in to help accommodate the influx of guests at the Homosassa Springs restaurant. "We have a big responsibility," Tim Sparks, president of Wichita, Kansas-based Daland Corp., which operates 82 dine-in Pizza Huts, told Fox News Digital. "We always want to provide great service, and we always want to provide a great product. But when you get put under a spotlight like this, and people are coming from two or three hours away, you've got to deliver on that expectation." PIZZA HUT BRINGS BACK VINTAGE VIBES AS FRANCHISEES EMBRACE NOSTALGIC MAKEOVERS Pizza Hut started the Classic initiative around 2017, according to Sparks. "They approached a few franchisees and said, 'Hey, we're thinking about doing this retro look. Do you guys want to participate in the test?' So I jumped at that opportunity," he said. The first Pizza Hut Classic that Daland opened was in Dahlonega, Georgia. "We flew out to see it once it was finished, and as soon as I walked through the door, it just really struck me," Sparks said. "I was super excited. I thought I was going to like it. I didn't know I was going to like it as much as I did. For me personally, it hit home." Leadership changes at Pizza Hut eventually led the brand to move away from the Classic remodels, Sparks said, but Daland was allowed to continue with them. "We did eventually run into a problem where we actually bought all the Tiffany lights that we could find," he said. "The brand quit producing them for us because … there just wasn't a big enough commitment from people to buy them." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Some of Daland's Pizza Hut Classic locations still don't have the distinctive lamps, but renewed interest in the retro restaurants could soon change that. "Now, because of the attention, we have five different vendors bidding to build those lights for us again," Sparks said. Customer feedback showed that the throwback styling "really resonated with everybody," Sparks said. Daland currently operates 39 Pizza Hut Classic locations. Since the Homosassa Springs restaurant was converted, dine-in sales have more than doubled, FOX 13 Tampa Bay reported. "Tons of people" travel from well over an hour away to visit the Pizza Hut Classic that Daland operates in Tunkhannock, Pennsylvania, which has attracted significant attention on social media, according to Sparks. "There's only 1,700 people in that town, and they will almost double the national average of Pizza Hut this year in sales," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Older generations with fond memories of Pizza Hut aren't the only ones drawn to the retro restaurants. Sparks said he encountered skepticism early on from those who believed the concept would primarily cater to baby boomers. "That's where they were dramatically wrong," he said. "When we started to get a lot of traction with social media, these weren't 50- and 60-year-olds coming in and doing TikToks, right? These were [people in their] teens and 20s coming in and doing them." As a kid, Sparks said, he was drawn to the music, diners and drive-ins of his parents' generation in the 1950s and 1960s. "It wasn't something I ever experienced because it was gone by the time I became a teenager, but it was something I always saw in pictures and really wished I had," he said. He believes younger generations may feel a similar pull toward the Pizza Hut Classics. "I think it does take them back to a little clip of time and an era where, in their minds, things weren't as hectic," Sparks said. "It was a little simpler time." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Sparks has also noticed another phenomenon when customers visit the Classic restaurants. "People put their phones down," Sparks said. "Once they're over the excitement, and they're taking pictures of the Pac-Man machine and the salad bar and the Tiffany lights … they set it down, and they start having conversation," he said. "I can't explain it, but it's super cool to watch." While Daland won't necessarily convert all of its Pizza Huts into full Classic restaurants, Sparks said the company plans to introduce retro elements — including Tiffany-style lamps and red cups — at its locations. He also plans to bring back the old red curtains at the Tunkhannock location. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "That would really take it all the way back," Sparks said.

articles.title: Nicole Kidman empezó a hacerse dermaplaning porque pensaba que era "como afeitarse" y ahora dice que nota mejor sus cosméticos
articles.summary: Rachel Keys, enfermera experta en dermocosmética, explica qué hay de cierto en esa sensación y cuándo este tratamiento puede convertirse en un problema
articles.body:
Nicole Kidman lleva décadas cambiando de piel delante de una cámara. Pelucas, prótesis, maquillaje, transformaciones físicas y personajes en los que cuesta reconocerla. Pero cuando se apagan los focos, la actriz parece buscar justo lo contrario: sentirse ella misma. A sus 59 años, esa relación con su imagen también ha cambiado y, en una reciente entrevista con Allure , ha contado uno de los últimos gestos que ha incorporado a su rutina de belleza: el dermaplaning .

"Empecé a hacerlo hace aproximadamente un año", explica Kidman, que reconoce que durante mucho tiempo tuvo reparos porque pensaba que era "como afeitarse". Ahora asegura que nota que su hidratante se aplica con más facilidad y también los sérums que utiliza. Siente que consigue una exfoliación natural.

La experiencia de la actriz plantea una pregunta bastante más interesante que copiar o no su rutina: ¿realmente los cosméticos funcionan mejor después de un dermaplaning o simplemente parece que lo hacen? Rachel Keys, enfermera experta en dermocosmética, aclara que hay una diferencia importante entre ambas cosas.

El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es simplemente "afeitarse la cara"

Es normal que se relacione porque se parecen. En ambos casos hay una cuchilla involucrada que pasa sobre la superficie cutánea y elimina el vello fino. Pero eso es todo lo que tienen en común. "El dermaplaning es, básicamente, una exfoliación superficial que se realiza con una cuchilla específica y estéril. Además de retirar el vello fino de la cara, elimina células muertas de la capa más superficial de la piel", explica Rachel Keys.

Ese segundo efecto es el que marca la diferencia. Mientras que al afeitar el rostro en casa el objetivo principal suele ser retirar el vello, con el dermaplaning se busca también trabajar la textura cutánea mediante una exfoliación mecánica superficial. Al eliminar parte de las células acumuladas y el vello fino, la superficie queda más uniforme y suave . Y esa nueva textura cambia también cómo sentimos cualquier producto que aplicamos después.

Por qué Nicole Kidman nota que sus sérums funcionan mejor después del 'dermaplaning'

Que un sérum se deslice mejor o parezca integrarse de manera diferente sobre la piel no significa necesariamente que sus principios activos hayan multiplicado su eficacia. " Estamos dejando una superficie mucho más lisa . Al retirar el vello y parte de las células acumuladas, el sérum o la crema se deslizan mejor y se reparten de una forma más uniforme", explica Keys. De ahí esa sensación inmediata de "piel nueva" , más suave y luminosa, que puede hacer que percibamos incluso nuestros cosméticos habituales de otra manera.

¿Penetran más? La experta pide prudencia. "Puede facilitar ligeramente el contacto de los productos con la piel , pero no diría que el dermaplaning hace que todos los activos penetren mucho más ". Es decir, Nicole Kidman no se equivoca cuando dice que nota mejor la aplicación de sus hidratantes y sérums. Lo que es incorrecto es convertir esa experiencia sensorial en la promesa de que cualquier principio activo va a funcionar más por haber pasado antes una cuchilla por el rostro. "No debemos pensar que, por hacernos dermaplaning , un sérum va a multiplicar su eficacia" , resume Keys.

El 'dermaplaning' de Nicole Kidman no es una buena idea para todas las pieles

Que una actriz diga que algo le funciona no convierte ese tratamiento en universal. Según Keys, puede ser especialmente interesante cuando existe bastante vello facial fino , una textura irregular o esa apariencia apagada que muchas veces buscamos corregir mediante exfoliación. Sin embargo, hay pieles en las que retirar mecánicamente la capa más superficial puede conseguir justo el efecto contrario al deseado .

"Si tenemos una piel muy sensible, rosácea, dermatitis , acné inflamatorio o la barrera cutánea está irritada, podemos provocar más rojez y sensibilidad", advierte. Su recomendación en esas circunstancias es primero recuperar la piel y después plantearse exfoliarla. La barrera cutánea irritada no necesita que hagamos más cosas; en muchas ocasiones necesita que dejemos de hacerlas. La exfoliación, además, no tiene una única forma. Existen alternativas químicas y enzimáticas con mecanismos diferentes, y su elección debe adaptarse al estado y las necesidades de la piel.

Cada cuánto hacer el dermaplaning de Nicole Kidman y qué no ponerse después

Otro error sería interpretar una piel más lisa como una invitación a repetir el tratamiento continuamente. Keys sitúa una frecuencia orientativa de una vez cada tres o cuatro semanas , siempre condicionada a que la piel lo tolere correctamente.

Pero casi más importante que lo que hacemos durante el dermaplaning es lo que hacemos después. "Me olvidaría durante unos días de hacer cosas a la piel: nada de exfoliantes, retinoides ni ácidos potentes", recomienda la experta. Tras una exfoliación de este tipo, propone volver a lo básico con una rutina hidratante y calmante. Y hay un producto que no admite negociación: fotoprotector SPF 50 todos los días. " La piel recién exfoliada agradece mucho más la calma que una sobredosis de activos", sentencia Keys.

Lo que sí puede hacer que tus cosméticos penetren mejor

Una cosa es que un cosmético se deslice mejor después del dermaplaning y otra que esté formulado para conseguir que sus activos lleguen más lejos. La cosmética más avanzada ya trabaja precisamente en esto, buscando formas de atravesarla o modularla de manera controlada.

Entre las tecnologías que más están dando que hablar están los liposomas, que encapsulan los activos para protegerlos y favorecer su distribución; las moléculas de bajo peso molecular; las microagujas cosméticas o espículas ; y la Keratinasa PB333 , una enzima obtenida mediante ingeniería genética que crea pequeñas vías de paso entre las células más superficiales sin comprometer la función protectora de la piel.

Esta última la he probado personalmente en las monodosis de SmartKer, igual que los sérums con microagujas cosméticas, y son dos tecnologías que me han resultado especialmente interesantes porque están pensadas para aplicar en formato sérum solas o antes de tus productos habituales ya que son capaces de ayudar a la penetración de los ingredientes de estos.

Como explica el químico y doctor en Nanomedicina Arturo Álvarez-Bautista, la nueva cosmética busca "aumentar la biodisponibilidad" y aumentar su permanencia en la piel.
